items.title: The 17 SDGs replaced the 8 Millennium Development Goals in 2015
items.claim: What are the UN Sustainable Development Goals?

options.text: A binding international treaty signed by all nations
17 goals with 169 targets agreed by UN member states in September 2015, to be met by 2030 — covering poverty, education, climate, gender equality and others; non-binding but with national reporting

items.reveal:
The Millennium Development Goals (2000-2015, 8 goals, 21 targets) focused on poverty reduction in LICs. The SDGs (2015-2030, 17 goals, 169 targets) apply universally — HICs are also measured.

Progress is monitored through Voluntary National Reviews. The UN's annual SDG report tracks the 232 indicators. The COVID-19 pandemic reversed progress on several goals; the UN reports that the world is not on track for any of the 17 goals at projected 2030.

The SDGs replaced the MDGs partly because the latter were criticised for being designed by HICs for LICs without sufficient consultation.
items.why: The architecture of international development matters. Whether progress targets are set globally and how they are measured shapes national policy priorities — even when there is no enforcement mechanism.

items.title: Tokyo is the world's largest urban area at around 37 million
items.claim: How many megacities exist and which is largest?

options.text: Around 33 megacities (cities over 10 million inhabitants) as of 2022; Tokyo is largest at around 37 million, followed by Delhi (32 m), Shanghai (28 m), Dhaka (23 m), São Paulo (22 m)

items.reveal:
UN World Urbanization Prospects (2018, updated 2022) lists 33 megacities. Largest by metropolitan area: Tokyo (37 m), Delhi (32 m), Shanghai (28 m), Dhaka (23 m), São Paulo (22 m), Cairo (22 m), Mexico City (22 m), Beijing (21 m), Mumbai (21 m), Osaka (19 m).

Lagos (Nigeria, around 15 m) is the fastest growing — UN projections suggest it could exceed 30 m by 2050. By 2050, around 50 megacities are projected, most in Africa and South Asia.

Definitions matter: 'city proper' versus 'urban agglomeration' versus 'metropolitan area' produce different rankings.
items.why: The geography of global population has shifted. 19th-century urban hierarchies (London, Paris, New York) no longer describe reality. The major cities of the 21st century are largely in countries that were poor a generation ago.

items.title: Spearman's rank correlation goes from -1 to +1
items.claim: What does Spearman's rank correlation coefficient measure?

options.text: The strength and direction of monotonic association between ranked variables, between -1 (perfect negative) and +1 (perfect positive); 0 indicates no monotonic relationship
The mean of the two variables

items.reveal:
Spearman's ρ uses ranks rather than raw values, making it robust to outliers and non-linear monotonic relationships. Pearson's r requires a linear relationship and normally-distributed data.

Critical values must be checked against sample size: with n=10, ρ must exceed about 0.564 to be significant at p=0.05. With n=30, the threshold is about 0.306.

A strong correlation can be coincidental, confounded by a third variable, or reversed in direction (Simpson's paradox). 'Correlation does not imply causation' is a methodological starting point, not a slogan.
items.why: Statistical reasoning is part of geographical skills. Strong correlation is evidence, not proof — geographers must argue causation separately from association, ideally through mechanism.
